title: Constantine (312–313)
hook: the emperor's victory, the Edict of Milan, and a freedom that brought new temptations

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great persecution, churches torn down and scriptures burned. Your line was they hid the books. Which verse did you read slowly? Day seven hundred sixteen.

Two Christian writers of the emperor's own time tell the same story, and they don't tell it the same way. Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the throne. Lactantius says he was told in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. Eusebius, writing later, says Constantine told him, and swore to it, that he saw a sign of light in the sky, a cross above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. Either way, he wins. And the world of the persecuted Church turns upside down.
screen: `TWO WRITERS, ONE STORY.` → `A SIGN ON THE SHIELDS.` → `BY THIS, CONQUER.`

segments.voice: First, the sign. It's honest to say the sources differ: a dream in one, a vision in the sky and then a dream in the other. What they agree on is that Constantine put a Christian sign on his army, and credited his victory to Christ. Second, the letter. Afterward, Constantine and his fellow emperor Licinius agree on a policy, and Lactantius copies the letter that announces it. It grants to Christians, and to all others, the free choice to follow whatever worship each person wants. Church buildings and property taken in the persecution are to be given back. People call it the Edict of Milan. Remember Nicomedia, and the books burning in the market square. Now Christians can ask for their churches back. Third, the surprise. Freedom was a gift, and it came with new temptations. The emperor gave the church money, buildings and favor. Bishops found themselves near the throne. Being Christian became useful for a career. Eusebius himself, who admired Constantine, complains in his Life of Constantine about hypocrites who slipped into the Church to win the emperor's goodwill. And Constantine, Eusebius says, was baptized only near the end of his life. Fourth, why it matters now. Persecution asks one question: will you stay? Comfort asks a quieter one: why are you here? The Church after Constantine had to learn to answer the second question.
screen: `TWO TELLINGS OF ONE SIGN.` · `FREEDOM FOR CHRISTIANS AND ALL OTHERS.` · `NEW TEMPTATIONS.` · `WHY ARE YOU HERE?` · then, large: `FREEDOM, AND ITS DANGERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what comfort does to faith. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a stretch of your life when things were hard, and then to a stretch when things were easy. In each one, where was your attention? On God, on the people you love, on what matters most to you? Don't judge it. Just notice what changed, if anything did. Then look at today. Is anything comfortable crowding out something that matters? If you pray, you can bring that to God honestly. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. The emperor who won under a Christian sign, granted freedom of worship, and brought the Church both peace and new temptations. Today's word.
Your line: freedom, and its dangers. Today, notice one comfort you lean on, and ask the quiet question: why am I here? Day seven hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: In Catholic tellings of Church history, Constantine's reign marks the end of the great persecution and the start of the Church's public life in the empire, with new freedom and new temptations.

original.note: Greek: by this, conquer — the words Eusebius says came with the sign. In Latin: in hoc signo vinces.

trapdoor: what you thought: when the persecution ended, the Church's troubles ended too.
what it means: freedom brought new temptations: money, power, and people joining for advantage.
what a scholar hears: Lactantius 44 and 48, and Eusebius's Life of Constantine, which tell the sign differently.

notes: Lactantius 44 (dream, heavenly sign on shields) and 48 (the letter of Constantine and Licinius: free choice for Christians and all others; property restored) paraphrased. Confirm.
Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.28–31 (Constantine's sworn account of a cross of light above the sun with 'by this conquer', the dream, the labarum) paraphrased. Confirm.
Eusebius, Life of Constantine 4.54: complaint about the hypocrisy of those who slipped into the Church for the emperor's favor. Confirm section and framing.
Baptism near the end of his life: Life of Constantine 4.61–62. Confirm.

Editor: 'two writers who knew the emperor' to 'of the emperor's own time' (the cited texts don't establish that Lactantius knew him); 'the same Christians can walk back into their churches' to 'can ask for their churches back' (the Nicomedia church was leveled; the letter orders property restored); howItsDone no longer speaks for 'Church historians' as a group.
Editor 2: cut the uncited sweeping tail 'and it has kept having to answer it since'.

Audit (y3 auditor): howItsDone 'the end of the persecutions' to 'the end of the great persecution' (Licinius later persecuted in the East, and Julian's reign followed). Lactantius 44 and 48, Eusebius VC 1.28 and 4.54 checked.
